title: Sports Centre, Festival, Urban Birds and Ice Houses

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Good morning, Riverside Sports Centre. How can I help you?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Hi, I'd like to join. I know the centre on Mill Road is a bit cheaper, but yours is only five minutes' walk from my office, so it's ideal.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Lovely. Can I take your name?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Daniel Hartley. That's H-A-R-T-L-E-Y.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: And your postcode?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: It's BR4 7TN.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: We have full, off-peak and weekend memberships. Full is forty-five pounds a month; off-peak covers weekdays before four in the afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: I usually train at lunchtime, so off-peak would suit me.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Then that's thirty-two pounds a month. Which activity are you most interested in?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: I used to play squash, but my knee isn't great any more, so it'll mainly be swimming.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: When would you like to start?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Could I start on the tenth of March?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: The pool is closed for maintenance that week, so how about the fourteenth?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: The fourteenth of March is fine.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: On your first visit, please bring proof of address, such as a utility bill. You don't need a photograph; we take one here.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: You'll also have an induction with a trainer. It used to take an hour, but now it lasts forty-five minutes.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Will my card be posted to me?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: No, we stopped posting cards. You'll collect it at reception when you come in for the induction.

transcript.speaker: Organiser
transcript.text: Thanks for coming to this briefing about the Greenfield Community Festival. Normally we hold it in the town park, but the park is being re-turfed, so this year we're moving to the school field.

transcript.speaker: Organiser
transcript.text: Gates open at ten for stallholders, but the festival begins officially at eleven, and it runs until late evening.

transcript.speaker: Organiser
transcript.text: Last year we raised money for the playground. This year every penny goes towards repairs to the community hall roof.

transcript.speaker: Organiser
transcript.text: Parking near the school is very limited and the station car park will be full, so please come by bus. There will be extra buses every twenty minutes.

transcript.speaker: Organiser
transcript.text: The food market and the dog show are back, of course, but the big new attraction is a climbing wall, run by instructors from the leisure centre.

transcript.speaker: Organiser
transcript.text: Children's activities, including face painting, will be in the yellow tent, next to the main stage.

transcript.speaker: Organiser
transcript.text: Our cooking demonstration was going to be at two, but the chef can only arrive later, so it will now start at three.

transcript.speaker: Organiser
transcript.text: Volunteers, please wear the green badge you'll receive today, not the blue one from last year.

transcript.speaker: Organiser
transcript.text: If a child gets lost, staff will take them straight to the information point by the main gate.

transcript.speaker: Organiser
transcript.text: We decided against fireworks because of the animals nearby, so the festival ends with a lantern display on the field.

sections.title: A student project on urban birds

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: So, Tom, our tutor asked why we picked urban birds. Honestly, it wasn't her idea, and I'd never been into birds before. We chose it because the data is so easy to collect: we just record outside our flats.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: True. I still think the questionnaire we sent to residents was far too long, though. The design was fine, but half the people gave up before the end.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: And the first survey site was a disaster. There were plenty of birds and the noise was manageable, but the gates were locked most days, so we couldn't get in.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: We have notes on feeding and nesting, but I think the report should focus on how the songs have changed. That's where our data is strongest.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: I'll make the charts, since I'm quicker with the spreadsheet. Could you write the introduction and email the expert at the museum?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Sure. The key finding is that city birds sing at a higher pitch, so their songs aren't drowned out by low traffic noise.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: And we should mention that all the recordings were made early in the morning, before the roads got busy.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: We analysed the sounds with free software from the university, rather than the expensive app the tutor mentioned.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Then we compare our results with the study from Berlin. The one from Paris used different species, so it's less useful.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: The final report is due next month, but the draft has to be in by Friday. Let's aim for Thursday, just in case.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Today I want to look at how people kept ice before refrigeration. In winter, ice was cut from frozen lakes and rivers and stored in buildings called ice houses.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Most ice houses were built partly underground and had an egg shape, which allowed the melting ice to slide down and stay compact.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The walls were lined with straw, which kept out the warm air. Sawdust was tried later, but straw remained the most common choice.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: At the bottom there was always a drain, because standing water would melt the rest of the ice very quickly.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Ice was expensive, so it belonged mostly to wealthy families, who used it mainly for desserts such as ice cream and chilled fruit.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Doctors were also customers: they used ice to bring down a fever, long before modern medicines were available.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In the nineteenth century, local ice was no longer enough. Some was shipped from America, but most of Britain's ice was imported from Norway.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: From the ports, the ice was moved inland by train, which was much faster than the old canal boats.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The trade declined quickly after the invention of the refrigerator, and by the 1930s most ice houses had been abandoned.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Today, many surviving ice houses are protected, and their cool, dark interiors make them ideal homes for bats.
